findings.body: AuditLogEntry.datetime is passed to math.floor or math.ceil, raising TypeError while building the cursor and returning an HTTP 500 instead of audit-log results.
findings.evidence: return int(math.floor(value) if self._is_asc(for_prev) else math.ceil(value))
findings.failure_mode: The opt-in pagination path crashes on the first non-empty page when build_cursor invokes the item-key callback.
findings.impact: AuditLogEntry.datetime is passed to math.floor or math.ceil, raising TypeError while building the cursor and returning an HTTP 500 instead of audit-log results.
findings.root_cause: The new paginator copies numeric cursor-key logic without preserving DateTimePaginator's datetime-to-microseconds conversion.
findings.suggested_fix: Reuse DateTimePaginator.get_item_key or convert the datetime to the existing microsecond integer representation before applying floor/ceil.
findings.title: Optimized paginator applies numeric rounding to datetime values
findings.trigger: An authorized administrator requests the audit-log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and at least one matching audit-log entry exists.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 840 exists verbatim: `return int(math.floor(value) if self._is_asc(for_prev) else math.ceil(value))`. The patch introduces OptimizedCursorPaginator with get_item_key that applies math.floor/ceil to `getattr(item, self.key)`. When used with AuditLogEntry ordered by `-datetime`, the key is a datetime object. math.floor/ceil require numeric types and will raise TypeError on datetime. DateTimePaginator (L230-236) converts datetime to microseconds first, but OptimizedCursorPaginator lacks this conversion. Trigger is realistic: admin requests audit-log with optimized_pagination=true and results exist.

findings.body: The integer cursor value is passed into the datetime field filter instead of being converted back to a datetime, causing field conversion/database errors or an incorrect page rather than continuing pagination.
findings.failure_mode: Subsequent optimized pages cannot reliably construct the cursor-filtered queryset.
findings.impact: The integer cursor value is passed into the datetime field filter instead of being converted back to a datetime, causing field conversion/database errors or an incorrect page rather than continuing pagination.
findings.root_cause: The new paginator overrides value_from_cursor with an identity function even though the endpoint orders by the datetime field.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement the same cursor-value conversion as DateTimePaginator, converting the serialized microsecond value back to a timezone-aware datetime before calling build_queryset.
findings.title: Optimized paginator does not convert datetime cursor values before filtering
findings.trigger: A request supplies a non-empty optimized pagination cursor for an audit-log query, such as a cursor containing the serialized integer datetime key.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 843 exists verbatim: `return cursor.value`. The patch shows value_from_cursor returns cursor.value directly (an integer microsecond timestamp from cursor serialization). When build_queryset uses this integer to filter the datetime field, Django will fail or produce incorrect results since datetime fields expect datetime objects, not integers. DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor (L226) converts the integer back to datetime. This is a distinct bug from candidate 0 - different method, different code path (cursor filtering vs item key generation), requires separate fix.

findings.body: Django raises ValueError because QuerySet slicing does not support negative start indices; the exception is not converted to a pagination parse error and the endpoint returns HTTP 500.
findings.failure_mode: A client-supplied negative cursor causes an uncaught server error instead of a valid page or controlled invalid-cursor response.
findings.impact: Django raises ValueError because QuerySet slicing does not support negative start indices; the exception is not converted to a pagination parse error and the endpoint returns HTTP 500.
findings.root_cause: The new advanced-offset branch assumes Django ORM negative slicing is supported.
findings.suggested_fix: Reject negative cursor offsets with BadPaginationError, or implement reverse traversal using supported queryset ordering and non-negative slices rather than passing a negative slice bound.
findings.title: Negative optimized offsets use unsupported Django queryset slicing
findings.trigger: An authorized administrator requests optimized pagination with a cursor whose offset is negative, causing the enable_advanced_features branch to set start_offset to that negative value.
findings.verifier_reason: Line 882 exists verbatim: `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. The patch at L877-882 explicitly allows negative cursor.offset when enable_advanced_features=True, setting start_offset to the negative value. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices and raises ValueError. The comment at L876 falsely claims Django handles negative slicing. Trigger: admin with enable_advanced_features=True sends cursor with negative offset. This is a distinct bug from candidates 0 and 1 - different root cause (negative slice) and different fix needed.
